summary: Discovery focused on embedding dimensionality, hybrid recall + rerank architecture, vector DB integration patterns, and ops constraints (throughput, shards, private VPC). Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private; main asks: cost/latency trade-offs, throughput baselines, and security controls.
topics: dedicated vs hosted vs private VPC
transcript: [00:00] Samira Khan: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time. I see Alex, Priya, Tom, Mei from BlueBridge and I'm joined by Diego and Rohit. Quick check — audio ok?
[00:06] Alex Cho: Yep can hear you. Thanks Samira. We pulled together a few folks because this is both infra and model work so wanted to align on constraints.

[00:12] Priya Sharma: Hi all. Quick background — BlueBridge runs an insights product, we index both docs and short snippets, currently ~12M embeddings, mostly 768d from a public encoder. We do a two-stage flow: ANN recall, then a cross-encoder rerank for top-k. Looking for options to move off our homegrown pipeline to reduce maintenance and improve latency/cost.

[00:28] Tom Reynolds: And from infra side we have an internal SRE team — we care about VPC, audit logs, and the ability to pin model versions. Also throughput: peak query bursts ~800 QPS, steady ~120 QPS, tail p95 must be <120ms for the recall stage, and end-to-end p95 <500ms on average unless rerank bump is expected.
[00:47] Diego Mendez: Thanks — that's super helpful. One quick clarification: the 800 QPS are that for raw k-NN lookups or includes the cross-encoder reranker?

[00:52] Priya Sharma: That's raw recall queries. Rerank is applied to top-30 results and runs on a GPU-based cross encoder. So the recall stage is latency-critical and we want batchability; rerank can tolerate a bit more latency but still needs to be predictable.

[01:05] Rohit Patel: From Redwood's side we commonly see two patterns: hosted API with vector DB on managed Pinecone/Redis/FAISS, or Redwood Dedicated where we co-locate the embedder and reranker on reserved GPU pools. For private installs you can run the control plane in a VPC and host inference on-prem. We'll map tradeoffs to your QPS and index size.
[01:28] Alex Cho: Great. We're especially curious about dimensionality. Right now 768 dims — any guidance on reducing dim or quantization? We care about recall + rerank interaction.

[01:36] Diego Mendez: Short answer: dozens of teams go down to 256 or 384 dims with retrained projection heads and see small recall delta when reranker is robust. Quantization (8-bit/4-bit) helps memory and cpu cache, but for ANN index quality you want to tune IVF/HNSW params. Also caching prefixes and top-k caches reduce repeated cost.
[01:50] Priya Sharma: Do you have internal guidance on dimension vs throughput numbers? We can't do a full experiment yet — need an estimate to present to leadership.

[01:58] Diego Mendez: We'll share a small benchmark template. Rough ballpark: 768d vectors in a sharded HNSW on CPU can do ~200-600 QPS per shard depending on efConstruction/efSearch, hardware. GPU-accelerated ANN or quantized indices push that higher. With Redwood Dedicated you can get higher guaranteed throughput due to reserved GPU pools and batch-optimized kernels.
[02:19] Tom Reynolds: You said 'per shard' — how does shard count affect memory and latency? We're wrestling with 12M vectors — what's an expected footprint?

[02:26] Rohit Patel: 12M x 768 floats uncompressed is about 36GB raw, plus index overhead. With PQ/OPQ and 8-bit quantization you can get under 10-12GB. Sharding splits both memory and qps; more shards equals more parallelism but more CPU and network coordination. For Dedicated we often co-locate index partitions with GPU inference nodes to minimize cross-node traffic.
[02:47] Mei Lin: Important for us: security. We need SAML SSO, customer-managed KMS for key rotation, and audit logs for indexing changes. Can Redwood Private satisfy that?

[02:56] Samira Khan: Yes — Redwood Private includes VPC control plane, KMS integrations, and audit logs. For hosted customers we support SOC2 controls and we can discuss bring-your-own-KMS for dedicated/enterprise plans. I'll link the security whitepaper after this call.
[03:07] Alex Cho: Another question — how do you typically integrate with existing vector DBs? We currently use an internal Redis/FC-ANN wrapper and are evaluating migrating to managed vector DBs.

[03:14] Diego Mendez: We see two integration patterns: 1) Redwood generates embeddings via API and you push vectors into your DB (we provide SDKs + sample batch loaders), 2) Redwood hosts both the embedder and reranker and exposes a retrieval API, with a sync connector to your vector DB. For migrations we often run a side-by-side A/B and a sample benchmark with your index format (Pinecone/Milvus/Redis/FAISS).
[03:33] Priya Sharma: For the reranker—do you recommend bi-encoder + cross-encoder or a hybrid? We want to reduce GPU cost on rerank.

[03:40] Diego Mendez: Bi-encoder for recall, cross-encoder for final quality is common. Cost optimization: use a small bi-encoder candidate scoring on CPU tier (or quantized GPU) to cut down the top-k for cross encoder. Redwood Optimize can suggest batching policies and quantization profiles per workload.
[03:55] Tom Reynolds: On the hosted plan, what's the SLA and what controls do we have around model pinning? If we want to pin a specific encoder version for the recall stage, is that supported?

[04:03] Rohit Patel: Hosted API supports model version pinning and you can configure per-route model preference. SLA varies by plan — we'll share the dedicated SLA for throughput and latency guarantees. For strict regulatory needs, Private is recommended where you control the deployment.
[04:13] Alex Cho: Can you give an example cost delta? If we move to dedicated with reserved GPU, how do we think about unit cost per query compared to hosted?

[04:20] Samira Khan: Costs vary by shape and commit. Roughly speaking, hosted is higher per-query but no ops overhead. Dedicated brings down per-unit inference cost with reserved capacity and burst pools. We'll include a sample cost model in the pricing sheet with a per-token and per-embedding baseline plus reserved GPU amortization.
[04:35] Priya Sharma: On latency, we saw in another solution the ANN recall was super fast but cross-encoder on GPU added ~250-400ms. Any approaches to reduce that without losing quality?

[04:44] Diego Mendez: Options: move cross-encoder to INT8/FP16 quantized kernels on GPU, use sequence-length reductions, or apply a two-stage rerank where a small transformer prunes to top-8 before the full cross encoder. Also batching at slight latency cost can increase throughput.
[04:59] Alex Cho: Do you support streamable responses for long-form reranks or is that only generation?

[05:05] Rohit Patel: Rerank responses are typically synchronous but you can stream intermediate scoring metadata. For long-form generation we support streaming; for rerank it's usually final scores returned for determinism.
[05:13] Mei Lin: Our compliance team needs data residency assurances — can Private be deployed on-prem or in our VPC region in EU-West?
[05:19] Samira Khan: Yes we have private deployment options and regional control for data residency. We'll capture your region preference in the follow-up.
[05:27] Priya Sharma: A bit of a technical nit — when you talk about automatic KV cache and prefix caching, does that apply to embeddings or only to generation tokens?

[05:34] Diego Mendez: Prefix/KV caching is primarily for autoregressive generation. For embeddings/ANN we do more request-level caching: materialized top-k for repeated queries, query fingerprint caches, and a short-term top-k store that avoids repeated compute for identical queries.
[05:48] Tom Reynolds: Our SRE is worried about node failure and index rebuild times — if a shard dies, what's recovery like?

[05:54] Rohit Patel: Recovery depends on index format; with replicated shards you get fast failover, but rebuilding from raw vectors can take hours. We recommend replication factor >1 for critical indexes and warm snapshots to quicker restore. For Dedicated we can provide cross-zone replication and snapshot scheduling.
[06:10] Alex Cho: Regarding metrics we need: per-query token cost, latency histogram, cache hit rate, and per-route cost breakdown. Does Redwood Console provide that?
[06:17] Samira Khan: Yes — Redwood Console surfaces per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, trace hooks, and custom alerting. We can show a sample dashboard in the SE deep-dive.
[06:26] Priya Sharma: Any gotchas migrating indices from our Redis wrapper to a FAISS-based topology?

[06:31] Diego Mendez: Two main items: format differences (float32 vs quantized) and parameter tuning for efSearch/efConstruction. Also watch for normalization differences and metadata reattachment. We provide migration scripts and a small compatibility harness.
[06:45] Tom Reynolds: On network architecture for Private, do we need to open inbound ports from Redwood or is it customer-initiated peering?

[06:52] Rohit Patel: We support customer-initiated VPC peering and private endpoints. For on-prem we ship an air-gapped package that talks only to your control plane if desired. We'll document the exact network flows.

[07:02] Alex Cho: Let's drill into the rerank compute math — if we have 800 QPS recall and top-30 rerank, naive cross-encoder would be 24k cross-encoder ops per second which is expensive. How do teams typically structure this?

[07:12] Diego Mendez: Exactly why most teams batch and prune. Approach: lower top-k to 8-12 via a stronger recall or a small neural candidate filter. Use FP16/INT8 on GPUs, adjust batch sizes for the cross-encoder so the GPU runs at higher utilization while keeping latency SLOs. For the extremes, consider a mixture: dedicated GPU pool for rerank, CPU/GPU mix for recall.
[07:31] Priya Sharma: For our replay and eval pipelines we need consistent embeddings. If you recommend dimension reduction, does that break historical vectors?

[07:38] Rohit Patel: It can. Typical pattern: keep historical index read-only and build a new index with reduced dims for new data while gradually re-embedding old items in the background, or run a one-time bulk re-embed when you can tolerate the cost.
[07:50] Alex Cho: Any reference numbers for memory savings from PQ/OPQ?
[07:53] Diego Mendez: PQ/OPQ can cut vector storage ~4-8x depending on codebook size. Combined with shard tuning you can fit much larger corpora into similar memory footprints.
[07:59] Mei Lin: On a process note: who would be our contacts for a pilot? We want a small POC with 100k vectors and synthetic traffic to validate the recall and the cost model.

[08:06] Samira Khan: I'd lead the pilot commercial side; Diego can run the SE benchmark and Rohit can help with private/dedicated mapping. We'll also include a solutions engineer for integration support.

[08:15] Alex Cho: Sounds good. For the POC scope: 100k vectors, 768d, 30k QPS ramp test seems too high — maybe 500 QPS peak for our test. We want a replayable query log and perf numbers at 95/99pctiles.

[08:27] Diego Mendez: Perfect. We'll prepare a benchmark plan: memory footprint, latency histograms for recall/rerank, and cost estimate for hosted vs dedicated. We'll also try a 384d projection as an optional arm.
[08:36] Tom Reynolds: A technical item — how does Redwood handle model fallbacks if a pinned model version is unavailable?

[08:41] Rohit Patel: Smart routing and automatic fallback policies exist — you can set a preferred model and fallback chain (e.g., quantized variant) and Redwood will route accordingly. We'll share the routing policy docs.
[08:52] Priya Sharma: Are there any differences in observability between hosted and dedicated? We need traces tied to our internal request IDs.
[08:58] Samira Khan: You can pass request IDs; both hosted and dedicated have tracing hooks and per-token tracing. Private gives you the most control over retention windows.
[09:06] Alex Cho: Competitor callouts — we've seen Pinecone claim low operational overhead, Milvus gives more control. Any migration friction you see specifically with Pinecone?

[09:14] Diego Mendez: Pinecone is easy for quick starts but can be limiting on custom index params. Migration friction tends to be around fine-grained index tuning and export/import nuances. We’ll run a sample migration test in the POC if you want.
[09:25] Mei Lin: Let's talk timelines — leadership wants a recommendation in 6 weeks. Can Redwood commit to a 2-3 week POC and a final recommendation in 6?

[09:32] Samira Khan: Yes, the typical cadence: week 1 kick off and data ingest, week 2-3 benchmark and tweak, week 4 slides and recommendation. We'll align resources if you sign a pilot statement of work.
[09:42] Alex Cho: Good. A couple of nitpicks — 1) We need to ensure any PII is masked in logs, and 2) we want a deployable infra diagram for our security folks.
[09:49] Rohit Patel: We'll include masking guidelines and a network diagram in the follow-up packet. Also will include sample IAM and KMS flows.
[09:58] Priya Sharma: One more technical: for HNSW efSearch tuning, do you help pick the parameters? We haven't tuned that deeply.
[10:04] Diego Mendez: Yes — SE team helps tune efSearch/efConstruction vs recall/latency tradeoff. We'll provide recommended defaults and run a grid search in the POC.
[10:13] Alex Cho: Ok let's summarize next steps then we'll open the floor for any quick clarifying questions.

[10:18] Samira Khan: Recap — Samira will send pricing + security docs; Diego will deliver a benchmark template and run an initial throughput calc; Rohit will map private/dedicated network options and recovery patterns; Alex to provide index stats and query log sample. SE deep-dive to be scheduled for week of 6/23. Any objections?
[10:33] Tom Reynolds: No objections from infra side.
[10:35] Mei Lin: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:38] Samira Khan: Great — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the artifact pack. Thanks all, talk soon.
[10:43] (call ends)
